title: Zariski splitting of solvable torsors and the underlying solvable variety
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $H$ a smooth connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. A split solvable group means a group admitting a finite series of smooth connected closed subgroup schemes, each normal in the preceding one, with successive represented group-sheaf quotients isomorphic to $\mathbf G_a$ or $\mathbf G_m$ [def-sc-gm-ga, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]; the quotients are sheafifications for faithfully flat finitely presented covers. Assume $H$ is split solvable. For every $k$-scheme $S$ [def-pc-scheme], every represented right $H$-torsor $P\to S$ for that topology is Zariski locally trivial: $S$ has an open cover $\{S_i\}$ with $P\times_SS_i\simeq S_i\times_kH$ equivariantly over $S_i$. A right torsor means a faithfully flat finitely presented map with right $H$-action and isomorphism $P\times_k H\to P\times_SP$, $(p,h)\mapsto(p,ph)$. There exist integers $r,s\geq0$ and an isomorphism of $k$-schemes $H\simeq\mathbf A_k^r\times_k(\mathbf G_m)^s$. Here $\mathbf A_k^r=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_r])$. For every extension field $K/k$, every invertible module on $H_K=H\times_k\operatorname{Spec}K$ is trivial; invertible means Zariski locally free of rank one [def-sc-invertible-module]. If $k$ is algebraically closed [def-weil-algebraic-closure], every smooth connected affine solvable $k$-group of finite type is split solvable; solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups become trivial.

source.place: Definition 6.33; Proposition 16.52 (Lie--Kolchin and splitting over a perfect field), printed p.343; Proposition 16.55(c) and Corollary 16.56, printed p.344. Picard triviality after field extension follows from the same displayed affine-space-times-torus scheme and the UFD argument in 16.56 and Appendix A.79, printed p.584.

proof.text: First treat $L=\mathbf G_a,\mathbf G_m$. An additive torsor has a section over every affine open by [lem-sfb-additive-affine-torsor-section]. For $L=\mathbf G_m$, apply [lem-sfb-split-torus-torsor-frame-geometry] with rank one: the torsor is the frame scheme of an invertible module. A local basis of that module is a section of its frame scheme [def-sc-invertible-module]. Thus these torsors are Zariski locally trivial; over an affine $S$ on which every invertible module is trivial they have a global section. In either case a section $e$ gives the equivariant isomorphism $(s,l)\mapsto e(s)l$: the torsor isomorphism in the statement, restricted to pairs whose first coordinate is $e(s)$, gives its inverse.

source.place: Example 2.72 and Proposition 16.55(a),(c), printed pp.61,344; rank-one frame description

proof.text: Induct on the length of a chosen split series, proving simultaneously: every torsor is Zariski locally trivial, and every torsor over an affine scheme with trivial Picard group has a section. Length zero is the trivial group $1=\operatorname{Spec}k$: the torsor isomorphism $P=P\times_k1\to P\times_SP$ is the diagonal, so $P\to S$ is a monomorphism; being flat and locally of finite presentation it is an open immersion by [lem-pe-flat-lfp-monomorphism-open], and being surjective it is an isomorphism, which is a global trivialization. For positive length put $N=H_1$. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] the quotient $q:H\to Q=H/N$ is a faithfully flat finitely presented homomorphism with scheme-theoretic kernel $N$ representing the fppf quotient, and $Q\cong\mathbf G_a$ or $\mathbf G_m$ by the given series; $N$ and $Q$ are affine of finite type. These are the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-normal-extension-torsor-reduction], so $R=P/N\to S$ is a represented $Q$-torsor. Step 1 gives sections of $R$ on a Zariski cover. For each section $a:T\to R$, $P_a\to T$ is an $N$-torsor, so the shorter-series induction gives sections on a further Zariski cover of $T$. Their compositions into $P$ are sections of $P\to S$. Over an affine $S$ with trivial Picard group, both choices are global: step 1 chooses $a$ and the stronger induction chooses a section of $P_a$. Translating these sections as in step 1 proves the required equivariant local trivializations.

source.place: Proposition 16.55, printed p.344: extension induction made explicit; Example 2.68, printed p.60

proof.text: For later use let $F$ be any field and $Z=\mathbf A_F^d$. It is Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian]: it is finite type over $\operatorname{Spec}F$, whose only ideals are $0$ and $F$, so that base is Noetherian [pqf-def-locnoeth]. The coordinate ring is a UFD by [lem-sfb-polynomial-field-ufd]. Every local ring is a prime localization of it by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-open-stalk-localization], hence a UFD by [lem-sfb-ufd-prime-localizations]. For any open $V\subseteq Z$, [lem-sfb-invertible-extension-factorial-complement] extends an invertible module on $V$ to $Z$. That extension is trivial by [lem-sfb-affine-space-invertible-trivial], so its restriction is trivial. This also covers $d=0$ and the empty open. In particular both $\mathbf G_a=\mathbf A^1$ and $\mathbf G_m=D(t)\subseteq\mathbf A^1$ are affine and have trivial Picard group.

source.place: Tag 0BDA (lemma-open-subscheme-UFD), Noetherian proof; Tag 0BD9 (lemma-extend-invertible-module); affine-space and punctured-line cases

proof.text: Induct again on the split-series length to describe the scheme $H$. The trivial group is $\mathbf A^0\times\mathbf G_m^0$. In the positive-length case, [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] makes $H\to Q=H/H_1$ an $H_1$-torsor. Step 3 shows that $Q\cong\mathbf G_a$ or $\mathbf G_m$ is affine with trivial Picard group. The global assertion of step 2, applied to the shorter group $H_1$, gives a section $s:Q\to H$ and the scheme isomorphism $Q\times H_1\to H$, $(q,h)\mapsto s(q)h$. By induction $H_1\cong\mathbf A^a\times\mathbf G_m^b$. Adding the factor $Q$ yields $(r,s)=(a+1,b)$ in the additive case and $(a,b+1)$ in the multiplicative case. These are scheme isomorphisms, so no assertion that this section is a group homomorphism is needed.

source.place: Corollary 16.56, printed p.344: torsor-and-affine-vanishing induction, using the given split series directly

proof.text: Base change the scheme isomorphism of step 4 to any extension $K/k$. The result is $H_K\cong\mathbf A_K^r\times\mathbf G_{m,K}^s$. In coordinates this is the principal open $D(t_{r+1}\cdots t_{r+s})$ of $\mathbf A_K^{r+s}$, with the empty product interpreted as $1$. Step 3 applies over the field $K$ and makes every invertible module on this open trivial. Pullback along the isomorphism and its inverse preserves local rank-one bases, hence gives the asserted triviality on $H_K$.

source.place: Corollary 16.56 and Appendix A.79, printed pp.344,584; apply the open-affine-space argument after extending the field

proof.text: Finally suppose $k$ is algebraically closed and $H$ is smooth connected affine solvable. Such a field is perfect: in positive characteristic every polynomial $T^p-a$ has a root, and in characteristic zero algebraic extensions are separable. Solvability in the statement's sense gives the series of that node: by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup] each derived subgroup $D^{i+1}=D_{D^i}$ of the smooth connected group $D^i$ ($D^0=H$) is a smooth connected normal subgroup of $D^i$, and $D^n=1$ for some $n$. The quotient $C=D^i/D^{i+1}$ is represented with faithfully flat quotient map $q$ by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]; the commutator morphism of $C$ composed with the faithfully flat $q\times q$ equals $q$ composed with the commutator of $D^i$, which factors through $D^{i+1}=\ker q$, so it is trivial and $C$ is commutative. Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] to obtain the smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup $U$ with torus quotient $D=H/U$. By the meaning of torus in that statement and algebraic closedness, $D\cong\mathbf G_m^s$. The coordinate subtori $D_j=1^j\times\mathbf G_m^{s-j}$ form a series with successive quotients $\mathbf G_m$. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], their inverse images in $H$ are smooth connected closed subgroups, normal in their predecessors, with those same quotients, and the last inverse image is $U$. Append the additive series of $U$ furnished by [lem-sfb-perfect-unipotent-additive-series]. This is the required finite split series from $H$ to $1$. It also works when $s=0$ or $U=1$.

source.place: Corollary 16.53 and Proposition 16.52, printed p.343; Theorem 16.33(a), printed p.335, and Corollary 16.24, printed p.331, spell out the final split series
